V. Narasingh,J.
1. Heard learned counsel for the Petitioner and learned counsel for the State.

2. This Criminal Revision has been filed under Sections 401 read with 397 of the Cr.P.C., assailing the judgment dated 02.12.2002 passed by the learned Addl. Sessions Judge (I), Dhenkanal in Criminal Appeal No. 30 of 1998 (422 of 2001), confirming the judgment dated 13.02.1998 passed by the learned Sub-Divisional Judicial Magistrate, Kamakhyanagar in 2(C) C.C. Case No. 101 of 1993 (Trial No. 139 1T of 1993), thereby convicting the petitioner under Section 16(1))(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954(hereinafter referred to as "the Act, 1954") and sentencing him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/-, and in default thereof, to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one month.
3. The Petitioner, being an accused, was prosecuted for selling adulterated chili powder for human consumption in his grocery shop and accordingly convicted and sentenced as aforesaid Sri. Santosh Kumar vs State Of Odisha on 9 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/106294141/

sentences.text: The plea of the Petitioner was one of denial and false implication.
To fortify their submission, the prosecution examined two witnesses P.W.1- the Food Inspector and P.W.2- Peon of C.D.M.O Office and several documents were exhibited and marked as. Ext. 1 to 9.
Though one witness was examined on behalf of the Petitioner- accused D.W.1 , no documentary proof was exhibited.

5. On an analysis of the evidence on record, the learned Trail Court found the Petitioner guilty of commission of an offence under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Act, 1954 and denying to extend the benefit of Probation of Offenders Act, 1958 directed him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/-, and in default thereof, to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one month.

6. Learned counsel Mr. Mishra, submits that both the learned Trial Court as well as the learned Appellate Court failed to take note of the statutory prescription contained in Section 10(7) and Section 13(2B) of the Act, 1954.

For convenience of reference the said provisions are extracted hereunder:
 "xxx xxx xxx  10. Powers of Food Inspectors.--
 (1) and (2) xxx xxx xxx (3) Where any sample is taken under clause (a) of sub- section (1) or sub-section (2), its cost calculated at the rate at which the article is usually sold to the public shall be paid to the person from whom it is taken.

( 4) to (6). xxx xxx xxx (7) Where the food inspector takes any action under clause (a) of sub-section (1), sub-section (2), sub-section (4), or sub-section (6), he shall, [call one or more persons to be present at the time when such action is taken and take his or their signatures].
 xxx xxx xxx  13. Report of Public Analyst.--
 (1) to (2A) xxx xxx xxx (2B) On receipt of the part or parts of the sample from the Local (Health) Authority under sub-section (2A)

, the court shall first ascertain that the mark and seal or fastening as provided in clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 11 are intact and the signature or thumb impression, as the case may be, is not tampered with, and dispatch the part or, as the case may be, one of the parts of the sample under its own seal to the Director of the Central Food Laboratory who shall thereupon send a certificate to the court in the prescribed form within one month from the date of receipt of the part of the sample specifying the result of the analysis.
xxx xxx xxx"

7. It is submitted by the learned counsel for the Petitioner, Mr. Mishra, referring to the judgment of the Appellate Court, that though the attention of the learned Appellate Court was specifically drawn Sri. Santosh Kumar vs State Of Odisha on 9 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/106294141/
2 to the infraction of Section 10(7) of the Act, 1954, the same was glossed over only referring to the evidence of P.W.1- the Food Inspector.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: So far as the 13(2B) of the Act, 1954 is concerned , there is no finding as such.

8. Per contra, learned public prosecutor submits that in the case at hand there is substantial compliance of Section 10(7) of the Act, 1954, since it is borne out from the record that the Food Inspector requested the persons present to act as witnesses but they declined.

So far as 13(2B) of the Act, 1954 is concerned, it is dependent upon the steps taken pursuant to Section 13(2) of the Act,
1954 and there is nothing on record to indicate that any objection was raised to the sample received under Section 13(2) of the Act, 1954.
Hence, the reference to Section 13(2B) of the Act, 1954 is misconceived.
9. It is the further submission of the learned counsel for the Petitioner that during the examination of the accused, the Petitioner was not confronted with the analysis report- Exhibit-7.
Therefore, the finding of the learned Appellate court that no prejudice was caused on the said account is an outcome of non-application of mind.
Hence, on that score, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside.
10. This Court perused the evidence of P.W.s.1 and 2 examined on behalf of the prosecution.

Though in the evidence of P.W.1, there is reference to an attempt to enlist independent witnesses, but the same has not been corroborated by P.W.2, who is an official witness and present with P.W.1 at the place of occurrence.

In the given facts, this Court is persuaded to hold that the said infraction goes to the root of the matter and since the safeguard contained in Section 10(7) of the Act, 1954 cannot be considered to be an empty formality.
Since nothing has been stated by the P.W.2 regarding independent witnesses, which goes to the Core of the matter, questions the very credibility of the prosecution cases.

11. The finding of the learned Trial Court in this regard as referred to in paragraph-7 of the Appellate Court's order, wherein, while adverting to the alleged infraction of Section 10(7) of the Act, 1954, the learned Appellate Court allowed its judgment to be clouded by mechanically relying only on the evidence of P.W.1.
There is no reference to the deposition of P.W.2 by both the Courts.

For convenience of ready reference paragraph-7 of the Appellate Court's order is extracted hereunder;
"xxx xxx xxx 7.
In the instant case, the Court below found that the appellant was dealing with food articles having a valid licence and accordingly, acquitted the appellant from the charge.

The Court below convicted Sri. Santosh Kumar vs State Of Odisha on 9 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/106294141/
3 and sentenced the appellant on the ground that he was selling adulterated food article i.e. chilli powder.

sentences.text: Perused the evidence of P.Ws.1 and 2 who are Food Inspector and a Peon working under him.
Both these witnesses deposed that they visited the shop of the appellant situated at Panduabar bazar.
It is also in the evidence of P.Ws.1 and 2 that the appellant was selling food articles in his shop to different customers at the time of their visit.
xxx xxx xxx

I have gone through the evidence of P.Ws.1 and 2 in careful manner The contention of the Counsel for the appellant is that the Food Inspector(P.W.1 has not called two or more witnesses to remain present at the time of taking sample of chilli powder from his shop and hence Sec.10(7) of the P.F. Act was violated.

In this connection, I have gone through the evidence of P.W.1 and found that he made effort to secure the attendance of two independent witnesses while taking sample of chilli posder from the appellant, but those two independent witnesses refused to become witnesses and hence he could procure their presence, Sec.10(7) of the P.F. Act provides a safe guard against false accusation.

Under this provision, the Food Inspector has obligation to call one or more persons to be present at the time of his taking sample of any article of food from a person selling such articles and he should obtained their signatures in token proof of the same.
In the absence of any such effort to secure the presence of any such person, the duty cast on the Food Inspector is not discharged.
In the instant Case P.W.1 states that he called the witnesses but they were not willing to cooperate and hence he could not take their signatures.
From the above, it is seen that the Food Inspector has done his duty and accordingly, the onus lies on him has been duly discharged.
Hence I find that the contention of the Counsel for the appellant is without any merit.
xxx xxx xxx"

12. The finding of the learned Appellate Court that the prosecution has been able to discharge the burden cast upon it under Section 10(7) of the Act, 1954, on the basis of the evidence of P.W.1, does not find favour with this Court.
13. In the light of such finding, it is not necessary for this Court to go into the other ancillary issues as raised.

Since the appreciation of the evidence by the learned Appellate Court as well as the learned Trial Court relating to infraction of mandatory prescription as contained in Section 10(7) of the Act, 1954 is found to be ex facie perverse, the judgment passed by the learned Trial Court as well as the learned Appellate Court are set aside.
The Petitioner is acquitted of the charges.
14. The Criminal Revision along with pending I.As, if any, is accordingly disposed of.

Bail bond(s)
stand cancelled and sureties are discharged.
